newsitem.title: UK: Sterling basks amid strong UK data, mark weakness.
newsitem.headline: Sterling basks amid strong UK data, mark weakness.

text.p: Sterling surged above 3.08 marks for the first time in more than seven-and-a-half years after new evidence of the strength of UK domestic demand added fuel to a rally driven this past week by moves in other major currencies.

Expectations that the UK monetary authorities will not step in anytime soon to halt the pound's rally means traders are looking for it to extend the 35 percent gains it has racked up against the mark in less than a year.
"These are heady levels but the trend is firmly in place and there is no solid reason to sell pounds," said a currency trader in London.
"The mark is getting hammered right, left, and centre and the danger is that people will keep running with the weak mark story."

Sterling rose as high as 3.0878 marks, the strongest it has been since September 1989. It was at 3.0748/58 at 1025 GMT from 3.0425/35 late Tuesday in Europe. Cable rose to $1.6810/20 from $1.6753/58 yesterday.

Expectations that European economic and monetary union will be launched by a broad group of countries have weakened the mark against currencies like the pound, the dollar and the Swedish crown which are not involved in the project.
The pound also tracked gains the dollar made against the mark after Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's Humphrey Hawkins testimony sparked a rally in U.S. assets yesterday.

"Sterling/mark's rise has been a factor of dollar/mark's gains recently," said Henry Wilkes, head of trading at Bank Julius Baer. "We are expecting dollar/mark to go to 1.85 which means sterling/mark can quite easily tackle 3.10."
Independent sterling strength surfaced, however, after a larger-than-expected increase in UK retail sales reinforced expectations that the Bank of England will raise rates in the coming months.

The report, which showed sales rose 0.6 percent in June and were up 5.4 percent from a year earlier, drove sterling up to 3.0878 marks, the strongest it has been since September 1989 and pushed cable up to $1.6861.
With economic fundamentals still favouring sterling bulls, traders expect the Bank of England will be wary of intervening to halt the pound's rally.

"Underlying demand is strong so it would be throwing good money after bad if the BoE were to intervene now," said Brian Martin, fx strategist at BZW. "The market will get itself long naturally and correct itself but for now 3.10 is possible."

Expectations that the UK monetary authorities are not about to get in the way of rampaging sterling bulls grew after Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown called on Tuesday for a stable and competitive pound but did not specify how he would achieve this goal.
"Brown's comments indicate they have not got a policy," said Wilkes at Bank Julius Baer.
Sterling's rise is hitting UK exporters hard and this may prove its undoing, analysts said.
Reuters Holding Plc and Courtaulds Plc said on Wednesday that their profits were hit by the pound's rise.
Also, British Steel said sterling strength was seriously impairing the competitiveness of many of its UK customers.
Sterling could therefore be vulnerable to a setback if June UK trade statistics published tomorrow show these concerns feeding through into a widening trade deficit, analysts said.
